I started in this business in nineteen eighty-eight, and people do not believe me when I describe it. We used to do everything on paper. Every order, every invoice, every credit decision. I would drive out to a farm on a Tuesday with a folder under my arm, sit at somebody's kitchen table for two hours, and drive back with a signature. Two hours for one signature, and I did that four times a week. What is strange is that I do not miss the paper at all, but I do miss the kitchen table. You used to learn things in those two hours that no system will ever tell you. You would see whether the machinery was maintained. You would notice that the son had left. Now I get a better file and a worse picture. If I could keep one thing from back in the day, it would not be the folder. It would be the drive home, when you had two hours to think about what you had just seen.

If you look at this sector across three decades, the shift that people talk about is technology, and I would argue that is the smaller half of the story. Yes, the paperwork was automated, and yes, a decision that used to take eleven days now takes about forty minutes. But the bigger change is who carries the risk. Thirty years ago the manufacturer sold to a distributor, the distributor sold to the farm, and each of them carried their own piece. Over time the chain compressed. Companies expanded, some of the middle disappeared, and the risk that used to be spread across four balance sheets now sits on one or two. That is why credit teams in this industry look completely different from how they looked in the nineties. They used to be an administrative function at the end of the process. Now they sit close to the beginning, because the decision about who gets product is, in practice, the decision about what the company is exposed to.
